reconstructed_theorem_text:
For every positive integer n, every nonnegative integer h, every i in {0,…,h}, and every deterministic family x = (x_j)_{j=0}^{h−i} of vectors in ℝ^n, the following law holds. Write [m] = {0,…,m−1}, set M = 2^{64(h+1)} and Q = 2^{74(h+1)}, and let P = {p ∈ {0,…,M} : p is even and p ≥ 4} and B = [h+1] × P. For k ∈ [h+1] let L_k = h−k+1 and T_k = ⨆_{j∈[L_k]} [Q^j], whose elements are pairs (j,t) with t ∈ [Q^j]. For (k,p) ∈ B define C(k,p) to be the set of all maps from [p] × T_k to [n]. Let I = ⨆_{(k,p)∈B} C(k,p), and let ξ be a standard Gaussian vector in the finite real Euclidean space ℝ^I (mean zero, identity covariance).

Set S_i = ∑_{j∈[L_i]} Q^j, and for p ∈ P set
a_{i,p} = 1 / (p^4 S_i^2 √(L_i log(2 M S_i))).
Here log is the natural logarithm and square roots are nonnegative. For u = (u_j)_{j∈[L_i]} in (ℝ^n)^{[L_i]} and η ∈ ℝ^{C(i,p)}, define
g(n,h,i,p;u,η) = √n a_{i,p} ∑_{α∈C(i,p)} η_α ∏_{(ℓ,(j,t))∈[p]×T_i} (u_j)_{α(ℓ,(j,t))}.
Let ξ^{(i,p)} be the unscaled coordinate restriction (ξ_{((i,p),α)})_{α∈C(i,p)} and let F(u,ξ) = ∑_{p∈P} g(n,h,i,p;u,ξ^{(i,p)}).

Write ρ(t) = exp(−1/t) for t > 0 and ρ(t) = 0 for t ≤ 0. Define
χ(r) = [ρ(r−13/20) / (ρ(r−13/20) + ρ(7/10−r))] · [ρ(1−r) / (ρ(1−r) + ρ(r−19/20))],
and let c = ∏_{j∈[L_i]} χ(‖x_j‖/√n), using the Euclidean norm. Define H(ξ) = 0 if any x_j is zero, and otherwise H(ξ) = c F((x_j/‖x_j‖)_{j∈[L_i]},ξ).

Then H is almost everywhere measurable under the standard Gaussian measure on ℝ^I, and its pushforward of that measure is the real Gaussian law of mean zero and variance max{n c² ∑_{p∈P} a_{i,p}², 0}. The expression inside the maximum is nonnegative, so the variance is n c² ∑_{p∈P} a_{i,p}². At variance zero this means the point mass at zero.
objects: The finite level-degree label set B, the inner index sets T_k and C(k,p), and the total Gaussian coordinate set I are as defined in the theorem. The deterministic ingredients are S_i, a_{i,p}, the glue function ρ, the cutoff χ, the scalar c, and Euclidean normalization. The scalar functions are the weighted block contraction g, the selected-level degree sum F, and the piecewise function H.
domains: n ∈ ℕ_{>0}, h ∈ ℕ, i ∈ [h+1], and x,u ∈ (ℝ^{[n]})^{[L_i]}, with [m] = {0,…,m−1}. P consists of even integers p with 4 ≤ p ≤ 2^{64(h+1)} (both bounds included). B = [h+1] × P, T_k = ⨆_{j∈[L_k]} [Q^j], C(k,p) = {α : [p] × T_k → [n]}, and I = ⨆_{(k,p)∈B} C(k,p). The block input η to g lies in ℝ^{C(i,p)}, the full ξ lies in ℝ^I, and χ, ρ, g, F, and H take real values.
quantifiers: Universally quantify deterministic n, h, i, and the entire family x in that order. For each such choice the displayed law is for the single random vector ξ with the standard Gaussian measure on the full ℝ^I. The auxiliary arguments u and η are arbitrary in their defining domains, and all sums and products are over all elements of the indicated finite sets.
assumptions: The only parameter restrictions are the given domains, in particular n ≥ 1 and 0 ≤ i ≤ h. No nonzero-vector, norm-bound, or unit-norm condition is imposed on x. The random input has the specified standard Gaussian measure; the zero-vector branch is part of the definition and not an excluded case.
conclusion: H is almost everywhere measurable for the standard Gaussian measure on ℝ^I, and its pushforward is the real Gaussian with mean zero and variance n c² ∑_{p∈P} a_{i,p}², represented as its nonnegative-real part. Variance zero gives the point mass at zero.
scopes: Although ξ has coordinates for every (k,p) ∈ B, F and H read only the restrictions ξ^{(i,p)} for the fixed selected i and p ∈ P, without any rescaling. The product in g runs over ℓ ∈ [p], j ∈ [L_i], and t ∈ [Q^j], using vector u_j at the coordinate α(ℓ,(j,t)). The cutoff product and the zero test each run over j ∈ [L_i]; if any x_j is zero then H is identically zero, and otherwise H uses the individual normalized x_j. This is a law for each fixed deterministic family, not a joint law over families or levels.
constant_dependencies: M = 2^{64(h+1)} and Q = 2^{74(h+1)} depend only on h; L_k = h−k+1 and S_i = ∑_{j∈[L_i]} Q^j. The factor a_{i,p} is exactly (p^4 S_i^2 √(L_i log(2 M S_i)))^{-1}, so depends on h, i, and p but not n, x, or ξ. The factor √n multiplies g and divides the Euclidean norms used in c. The first cutoff ratio uses 13/20 and 7/10; the second uses 1 and 19/20, with the exact arguments given in the theorem. The product c depends on the deterministic family and its index range, with no dependence on p or ξ.
